title: War & Conflict
content_html:
War Poetry in the Anthology

Four poems in the WJEC Eduqas anthology address war and conflict: Wilfred Owen’s Dulce et Decorum Est, Rupert Brooke’s The Soldier, Owen Sheers’s Mametz Wood, and Thomas Hardy’s A Wife in London. These poets span over a century of conflict, from the Boer War era to the trenches of World War I to a modern poet reflecting on the Battle of the Somme. Together they show how attitudes to war shift dramatically depending on experience, distance, and time.

Dulce et Decorum Est — Wilfred Owen

Wilfred Owen wrote Dulce et Decorum Est in 1917 while recovering from shell shock at Craiglockhart hospital. The poem describes a gas attack in vivid, horrifying detail, then directly attacks the “old Lie” that dying for one’s country is sweet and noble. Owen dedicated an early draft to Jessie Pope, a jingoistic poet who wrote cheerful recruitment verses encouraging young men to enlist.

Key Fact

The title comes from the Roman poet Horace: “Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori” — “It is sweet and fitting to die for one’s country.” Owen calls this “The old Lie,” capitalising “Lie” to emphasise his contempt for propaganda that glamorises war without acknowledging its true horror.

Key quotations: “Bent double, like old beggars under sacks” — the opening simile immediately destroys any heroic image of soldiers: they are broken, aged, dehumanised. “GAS! Gas! Quick, boys!” — the sudden shift to direct speech and short exclamations creates panic. “He plunges at me, guttering, choking, drowning” — the three present participles create a relentless, suffocating rhythm. The dream-like quality of “As under a green sea, I saw him drowning” uses the colour of chlorine gas to create a nightmarish underwater image.

Owen structures the poem in three movements: exhausted marching (slow, heavy rhythm), the gas attack (frantic pace), and the aftermath (direct address to the reader). The shift from third person (“they”) to first person (“I saw him”) to second person (“you”) draws the reader progressively closer to the horror. The final stanza’s address to “My friend” is bitterly ironic — Owen is not speaking to a friend but to those who perpetuate the “Lie.”

The Soldier — Rupert Brooke

Rupert Brooke wrote The Soldier in 1914, before experiencing combat. He died of sepsis in 1915 on his way to Gallipoli. The poem presents death in war as noble, peaceful, and transformative — the soldier’s body will make a “corner of a foreign field” that is “for ever England.”

Key quotations: “If I should die, think only this of me” — the conditional “if” and the imperative “think only this” invite the reader to consider death without fear. “A dust whom England bore, shaped, made aware” — England is personified as a mother who created and nurtured the speaker. “In hearts at peace, under an English heaven” — the final image presents death as eternal rest under a benign, familiar sky. There is no pain, no horror, no doubt.

Key Fact

Brooke wrote before experiencing combat; Owen wrote from the trenches. This difference in experience is the fundamental reason their poems present opposing views. Brooke’s idealism reflects 1914 patriotic fervour; Owen’s anger reflects 1917 disillusionment after years of mechanised slaughter.

Mametz Wood — Owen Sheers

Owen Sheers wrote Mametz Wood (2005) after visiting the site of the Battle of Mametz Wood (1916), where the 38th (Welsh) Division suffered devastating casualties during the Battle of the Somme. The poem describes farmers finding bones of soldiers surfacing from the earth decades later.

Key quotations: “The wasted young, turning up under their plough blades” — “wasted” carries a double meaning: lives wasted and bodies decomposed. “A mosaic of bone” — the fragments are beautiful and terrible simultaneously. “Their broken mosaic of bone / linked arm in arm” — even in death, the soldiers remain connected in comradeship. The earth is personified as gradually returning what it swallowed: “the earth stood sentinel.”

Unlike Owen or Brooke, Sheers writes about war from historical distance. He did not experience the fighting — he encounters its physical remains in the landscape. This gives the poem a meditative, elegiac quality rather than the immediacy of Owen’s work. The earth becomes a metaphor for memory: it preserves what happened and gradually reveals it, just as history resurfaces over time.

A Wife in London — Thomas Hardy

Thomas Hardy wrote A Wife in London (1899) during the Second Boer War. The poem’s two sections mirror two deliveries: first, a telegram announcing her husband’s death; second, a letter from him (posted before his death) describing his plans for their future together. The cruel irony of the sequence is the poem’s central device.

Key quotations: “She sits in the tawny vapour / That the City lanes have uprolled” — the fog creates a claustrophobic, isolated atmosphere. “Flashes of survey” describes the telegram announcing death — the military language (“survey”) dehumanises the loss. The second section’s letter contains “new love” and “hope to return” — words that are now impossibly painful because the reader already knows the outcome.

Experience vs distance: Owen writes from the trenches; Brooke from pre-war idealism; Sheers from a century later; Hardy from the home front. Each perspective shapes the poem’s attitude to war.

Glorification vs condemnation: Only Brooke presents war positively. Owen explicitly attacks those who glorify it. Sheers and Hardy show war’s lasting cost without overt political argument.

The body: Owen describes the body in agony (choking, drowning). Brooke transforms it into enriching “dust.” Sheers finds fragmented bones decades later. Hardy’s wife never sees the body at all — she receives only paper.

Key Fact

Hardy structures A Wife in London in two numbered sections that mirror the sequence of two deliveries. The cruel dramatic irony of receiving the death telegram before the hopeful letter creates devastating emotional impact without any explicit commentary.
exam_tip_html: When comparing war poems, consider the poet’s relationship to conflict: did they experience it directly (Owen), anticipate it idealistically (Brooke), encounter its traces (Sheers), or witness its domestic impact (Hardy)? This shapes everything from imagery to tone. Always analyse how the poem communicates its attitude — through structure, imagery, and form — rather than simply stating what the attitude is.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Owen uses visceral sensory imagery and direct address to expose the horror propaganda conceals; Brooke’s idealism reflects pre-combat innocence.
  • Sheers and Hardy explore war’s aftermath: bones surfacing decades later, and a widow receiving letters in the wrong order.
  • The key comparison skill is linking the poet’s perspective and context to their choice of language, imagery, and form.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Owen in 'Dulce et Decorum Est' and Brooke in 'The Soldier' present attitudes to dying in war.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses Owen's graphic imagery vs Brooke's idealised pastoral language. Compares sonnet form (Brooke's completeness vs Owen's disrupted structure). Links to 1914 idealism vs 1917 disillusionment with specific quotation analysis.

Secure: Clear comparison of attitudes with analysis of language choices.

Developing: Some comparison with relevant quotations.

Emerging: Simple statements about each poem.

practice_questions.text: How does Owen Sheers present the impact of war in 'Mametz Wood'?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses the earth-as-memory metaphor, the 'mosaic of bone' imagery, and how historical distance creates elegy rather than protest. Discusses the Welsh context and collective remembrance.

Secure: Clear analysis of key images and their effects.

Developing: Some relevant comments with textual support.

Emerging: Basic description of the poem's subject.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Hardy in 'A Wife in London' and Armitage in 'The Manhunt' present the impact of war on those left at home.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Contrasts Hardy's dramatic irony (two deliveries) with Armitage's gradual physical exploration. Both focus on women's experience of loss. Analyses how structure mirrors emotional experience in each poem.

Secure: Clear comparison with explained effects.

Developing: Some comparison with relevant references.

Emerging: Simple identification of similarities.

practice_questions.text: How does Owen use sensory imagery to convey the reality of war in 'Dulce et Decorum Est'?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses visual ('green sea'), auditory ('gargling'), tactile ('flung him in') imagery. Links to Owen's purpose of shocking complacent readers. Examines how pace shifts mirror the gas attack's chaos.

Secure: Clear analysis of specific images with explained effects.

Developing: Some relevant comments on imagery.

Emerging: Basic identification of descriptive language.

practice_questions.text: Compare how Brooke in 'The Soldier' and Sheers in 'Mametz Wood' present soldiers' bodies.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Contrasts Brooke's body as enriching 'dust' (abstract, positive) with Sheers's fragmented 'mosaic of bone' (physical, disturbing). Analyses how context shapes representation: pre-war idealism vs post-war archaeological discovery.

Secure: Clear comparison with analysis of imagery.

Developing: Some comparison with references.

Emerging: Simple description of each poem.

practice_questions.text: How does Hardy create dramatic irony in 'A Wife in London'?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses the two-section structure, the sequence of telegram then letter, and how the reader's knowledge creates pathos. Discusses Hardy's characteristic interest in cruel fate and timing.

Secure: Clear explanation of irony with textual support.

Developing: Some relevant comments on structure.

Emerging: Basic identification of events.

glossary_terms.definition: World War I poet (1893–1918) who wrote from direct trench experience and was killed one week before the Armistice.
Poet (1887–1915) who died before seeing combat; his war sonnets present an idealised, patriotic view of sacrifice.
Welsh poet (born 1974) whose work explores landscape, memory, and the relationship between past and present.
Victorian novelist and poet (1840–1928) whose work explores fate, suffering, and the cruelty of circumstance.
A situation where the audience knows something a character does not, creating tension or pathos.
Information, often biased or misleading, used to promote a political cause or point of view.
A poem of mourning or reflection on the dead, typically characterised by a meditative, sorrowful tone.
Language that appeals to one or more of the five senses, creating vivid mental pictures for the reader.
Extreme patriotism, especially in the form of aggressive or warlike foreign policy enthusiasm.
Giving human characteristics to non-human things, such as nature, objects, or abstract concepts.
